questions.question: Maya's class made a double bar graph of books read in October. On the graph, each square stands for 4 books. Maya's bar is 6 squares long. How many books did Maya read?
questions.explain: With many-to-one correspondence, multiply the number of squares by the value of one square: 6 × 4 = 24 books. A common trap is adding 6 + 4 = 10, or forgetting the scale and reading the bar as if one square meant one book.

questions.question: Liam's spinner is divided into 8 equal sections. 3 of the sections are red. If he spins it once, what is the probability that it lands on red?
questions.explain: Probability = favourable outcomes ÷ total equal sections, so P(red) = 3/8. The most common trap is writing 3/5 by comparing red sections to the not-red sections instead of to the total of 8.

questions.question: A double bar graph shows cans collected for a bottle drive. Each square stands for 10 cans. The Grade 5 bar is 7 squares long and the Grade 6 bar is 9 squares long. How many cans did Grade 5 collect?
questions.explain: Multiply the squares in the Grade 5 bar by the scale: 7 × 10 = 70 cans. On a double bar graph, check the legend first so you read the right bar — 90 is Grade 6's total, not Grade 5's.

questions.question: At a school water station, a double bar graph shows refills on Saturday and Sunday. Each square stands for 6 water bottles. The Saturday bar is 5 squares long and the Sunday bar is 8 squares long. How many MORE bottles were filled on Sunday than on Saturday?
questions.explain: Either find each total (8 × 6 = 48 and 5 × 6 = 30, so 48 − 30 = 18) or multiply the 3 extra squares by 6. The most common trap is answering 3, the difference in squares, without applying the many-to-one scale.

questions.question: Priya has a bag with 4 green marbles, 6 yellow marbles, and 2 purple marbles. Without looking, she pulls out one marble. What is the probability that it is yellow?
questions.explain: There are 4 + 6 + 2 = 12 marbles in all, so P(yellow) = 6/12 = 1/2. The usual trap is comparing yellow to the other marbles (6/6) or using the number of colours (1/3) instead of the total number of marbles.

questions.question: Noah's spinner has 5 equal sections and 2 of them are blue. He plans to spin it 40 times. About how many times should he predict it will land on blue?
questions.explain: P(blue) = 2/5, so predict 2/5 of 40: 40 ÷ 5 = 8, then 8 × 2 = 16 times. A common trap is stopping at 8 (that is only 1/5 of the spins) or guessing 20 because blue "feels like half."

questions.question: Aanya is rolling a fair 6-sided die in a board game. Amazingly, she has rolled a 5 four times in a row. What is the probability that her NEXT roll is a 5?
options: Less than 1/6, because 5 has already come up so many times
1/6, because each roll is independent of the rolls before it
More than 1/6, because this die seems to favour 5
4/6, because 5 came up 4 times out of the 6 numbers
questions.explain: Each roll of a fair die is an independent event: past results never change the next roll, so P(5) stays 1/6. The biggest misconception in this unit is thinking a number is "used up" or is "on a hot streak" — the die has no memory.

questions.question: A double bar graph shows money raised at a school fun fair. Each square stands for $15. Division 4's bar is 6 squares long and Division 5's bar is 4 squares long. The two divisions put all of their money together to buy soccer balls that cost $25 each. How many soccer balls can they buy?
questions.explain: First use the scale: 6 × $15 = $90 and 4 × $15 = $60, giving $150 in total, then $150 ÷ $25 = 6 balls. Two common traps are adding the squares (6 + 4 = 10) as if each square were one ball, and using only one division's money ($90 ÷ $25 → 3).
